strengths: Comprehensive and well-motivated end-to-end recipe covering data synthesis, trajectory curation, training strategy, and systems-level rollout infrastructure for data-analytic agents — a domain where open-source trained models are genuinely lacking.

Strong empirical results: DATAMIND-7B/14B achieve the best average scores among open-source models and even outperform proprietary baselines on three benchmarks, with a notably data-efficient training corpus (12K trajectories vs. 20K–2.5M for specialized baselines).

The analysis section (§5.3) provides several genuinely useful empirical insights: self-consistency filtering vs. trajectory selection, the dual role of SFT loss as stabilizer/culprit in RL (with entropy dynamics), and the cold-start/RL relationship. These are the most interesting parts of the paper and are supported by training-dynamics figures.

Good engineering contributions: chunked code maintenance for memory-frugal multi-turn rollout, void-turn filtering, and sandboxed isolated execution are practical and described at a reproducible level of detail.
Extensive appendix with full prompts, hyperparameters, baseline reproduction details, and a commitment to releasing data and models supports reproducibility.
Fair-comparison effort: trained baselines are reproduced on the same backbones (Qwen2.5-Coder-7B/14B), and benchmarks are format-normalized (converting tables to .sqlite).
weaknesses: Evaluation relies on GPT-4o-mini as judge for both training reward and test correctness, while the trained model is explicitly optimized to produce answers that satisfy this judge's criteria (format, length, conciseness). This creates a potential systematic bias in favor of DATAMIND over untrained proprietary baselines, and no human validation or judge-correlation study is provided.

Benchmark protocols are modified in ways that may weaken comparability: TableBench questions without gold answers are filtered, tables are format-converted, BIRD uses the validation set with exact match on materialized CSVs. The reported numbers are therefore not directly comparable to published results of the benchmarks.

Novelty is moderate: the hybrid SFT/RL loss with dynamic weighting closely follows Zhang et al. (2025b), RL uses off-the-shelf DAPO, and self-consistency filtering is a standard technique. The contribution is largely a careful system integration plus domain-specific data, which limits conceptual novelty.

Internal inconsistency: the paper's own analysis shows non-select (keeping all consistent trajectories) outperforms con-select (the shipped design) across datasets, yet DATAMIND-12K uses best-trajectory selection; the final models may be trained with a suboptimal configuration, and the insight is not reflected in the main system.

Ablations are limited and underpowered: RL runs are capped at ~350 steps, the cold-start analysis uses only 3,843 training samples and 240 test items, and no variance/confidence intervals or multiple-seed training runs are reported despite temperature-0.7 stochastic evaluation.

The claim of 'state-of-the-art... outperforming GPT-5' rests on a single-judge protocol with modified benchmarks and should be stated more cautiously; per-dataset margins over DeepSeek-V3.1 are mixed rather than uniform.
Scope restrictions are acknowledged (Qwen-family backbones only, ≤14B scale, reasoning-oriented tasks only, no visualization/predictive tasks), which narrows the claimed 'generalist' framing.

strengths: Tackles a practically important problem: training open-source, generalist data-analytic agents that handle heterogeneous file formats (csv/xlsx/sqlite) and multi-turn code execution, beyond simple table QA.

Provides an end-to-end, reasonably well-documented pipeline (query synthesis, knowledge-augmented trajectory sampling, self-consistency + rule-based filtering, hybrid SFT/RL training, memory-frugal multi-turn rollout) with prompts, hyperparameters, and reproduction details in the appendix.

Strong headline results: DataMind-7B/14B outperform reproduced specialized baselines (TableLLM, Table-R1, OmniSQL, SQL-R1) trained on much larger corpora, and reportedly exceed proprietary models on the authors' evaluation suite.

The analysis section (effect of self-consistency filtering, SFT loss as stabilizer/culprit for RL, cold-start vs. RL marginal gains) offers genuinely useful empirical insights for agent post-training, and the authors commit to releasing data, models, and code.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty. The core ingredients are assembled from existing work: ReAct scaffolding, DAPO for RL, and the dynamically weighted SFT+RL objective is explicitly adopted from Zhang et al. (2025b). The contribution is primarily an application/integration to the data-analysis domain rather than a new method.

Evaluation protocol raises fairness and validity concerns. (i) The same LLM judge (GPT-4o-mini) is used both as the RL training reward and as the evaluation metric, creating a train/eval coupling that plausibly inflates the gap in favor of DataMind models. (ii) Benchmark protocols are heavily modified: TableBench questions are filtered, tables converted to .sqlite/.csv, BIRD's validation set is substituted for its test set with exact match on materialized results. All reported numbers (including for GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3.1) come from this non-standard re-implementation, so the SOTA claim is not directly comparable to prior published results.

The claim of a 14B model beating GPT-5 and DeepSeek-V3.1 rests entirely on the above self-built protocol; no standard leaderboard or third-party verification is provided, and no statistical significance/variance is reported for the 3-trial pass@1 estimates.

Potential data contamination is insufficiently addressed: BIRD's training databases are used as a synthesis source while BIRD's validation set is an evaluation benchmark, and the same judgment model family is involved in both training-data curation and evaluation. No near-duplicate or contamination analysis is reported.

The 'scaling' framing is overclaimed relative to the evidence: only 12K trajectories, ~350 RL steps, a single model family (Qwen2.5-Coder) capped at 14B, and three benchmarks. There is no scaling curve over data size or model scale supporting the generality of the recipe.

Several design choices are justified only anecdotally (e.g., length-reward thresholds lmin=256/lmax=1024 'according to our observation', N=3 samples, the γ cosine schedule) without ablation; key ablations (Fig. 3, 6) are run on subsampled data or the 7B model only, limiting their support for the full 14B system.

Presentation issues: the informal 'raising a child' analogy and occasional promotional tone ('actionable insights', 'new state-of-the-art') sit awkwardly with the evidence; Figure 1a's taxonomy pie chart is largely unreadable; the paper's URL for code is a placeholder.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-motivated end-to-end recipe (data synthesis, trajectory curation, hybrid SFT+RL training, stable multi-turn rollout) addressing a genuine gap: strong open-source data-analytic agents built from scratch rather than prompted scaffolds over proprietary models.

Strong empirical results: DATAMIND-14B (71.16 avg pass@1) reportedly surpasses proprietary baselines including GPT-5 and DeepSeek-V3.1, and DATAMIND-7B outperforms all open-source baselines, using only 12K curated trajectories versus 20K-2.5M for baselines — an impressive data-efficiency result.

The analysis section (§5.3) provides genuinely interesting and honest empirical insights: the value of self-consistency filtering over best-trajectory selection, the double-edged role of SFT loss in RL stability (with entropy-curve evidence), and the RL-narrows-but-cannot-reverse base-model-gap finding. These are useful to the community.
Practical systems contributions (asynchronous rollout, chunked code maintenance, sandboxing, void-turn filtering) are well described and address real problems in code-based multi-turn agent RL.
Good reproducibility posture: code and a data subset submitted, hyperparameters and prompts fully disclosed in appendices, plans to release data and models.
weaknesses: Evaluation protocol deviates substantially from original benchmark metrics: GPT-4o-mini model-as-judge replaces accuracy/regex matching (DABench) and Rouge-L (TableBench), and BIRD's validation set replaces the official testbed. The headline claim of beating GPT-5/DeepSeek-V3.1 rests entirely on this judge-based evaluation, and the margin over DeepSeek-V3.1 is small (71.16 vs 70.58 pass@1), making the SOTA claim fragile; no analysis of judge agreement with gold metrics is provided.

Potential train/test contamination is not addressed: training files are harvested from Kaggle, and DABench files are Kaggle CSVs; query synthesis also uses BIRD training data while BIRD validation is used for testing. No de-duplication or overlap analysis is reported.

Limited technical novelty: individual components are largely assembled from prior work — DAPO (Yu et al.), ReAct, self-consistency filtering, and the dynamic SFT/RL weighting explicitly follows Zhang et al. (2025b). The contribution is more systems/engineering integration than new methods.

Internal inconsistency between analysis and the main method: §5.3 shows random-select and non-select match or beat the chosen con-select setting (partly attributed to larger training volume), yet the main results still use con-select; the recommended data-curation choice is not the one deployed.

The third insight (cold start vs. RL) is based on a very small evaluation (240 test items) and an arbitrary 3,843-sample training subset, and RL runs are limited to ~350 steps; the insight claims are suggestive rather than conclusive, as the authors themselves admit.
Backbone restricted to Qwen2.5-Coder 7B/14B family; no evidence the recipe transfers to other base models, and no statistical significance testing or variance reporting across the three trials.
Scope is narrower than 'generalist' suggests: predictive/modeling, visualization, and training-type tasks are excluded (acknowledged in limitations), yet the framing oversells generality.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-engineered end-to-end pipeline covering data synthesis, trajectory filtering, hybrid SFT+RL training, and a stable multi-turn code-execution rollout framework; the released DATAMIND-12K dataset and models are valuable resources for the community.

Strong empirical results: the 14B model (71.16% avg.) reportedly beats strong proprietary baselines (GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3.1) and all open-source alternatives, with a large margin over same-backbone baselines (11.26% -> 68.10% for 7B).

Thorough ablation and analysis sections: data-volume scaling, training-strategy comparison (SFT / zero-RL / SFT-then-RL / hybrid), self-consistency filtering vs. trajectory selection, gamma scheduling with reward/entropy dynamics, cold-start effects, and judge-model sanity checks. The empirical insights (e.g., SFT loss as both stabilizer and cause of collapse) are genuinely useful for practitioners.

Good transparency on evaluation fairness: re-scoring with an external judge (Qwen-2.5-72B, Pearson r=0.96), Rouge-L cross-check, data-contamination (header-overlap) analysis, and reproduction of baseline models under matched settings. Additional results on Llama backbone and QRData improve generality claims.
Clear limitations section and detailed appendices (hyperparameters, prompts, reproduction protocols) supporting reproducibility; commitment to release dataset, code, and models.
weaknesses: Limited methodological novelty: the individual components are largely assembled from existing work — DAPO (Yu et al., 2025), dynamic SFT/RL hybrid weighting (explicitly following Zhang et al., 2025b), self-consistency filtering, ReAct formatting, and standard GRPO-style agent RL. The contribution is primarily an engineering/systems integration applied to a new domain rather than a new technique.

Heavy circular dependence on GPT-4o-mini: it is used for trajectory filtering/selection, the RL reward (r_answer), and the primary evaluation metric across all benchmarks. The external-judge correlation check mitigates but does not eliminate concerns that the model is optimized toward the judge's biases, and judge reliability/error rates on descriptive answers are not quantified.

Evaluation protocol deviates from original benchmarks: TableBench converted from .json, trend-forecasting/chart questions filtered out, DABench's regex matching replaced with model-as-judge, and BIRD validation set used instead of the official test set. This weakens comparability with prior published numbers, although the authors re-evaluate baselines under the same protocol.

Training data scale is modest (11.7K trajectories) and synthesized by DeepSeek-V3.1 with judge-based filtering; the paper's claims about data quality driving gains are supported by ablations but the pipeline's potential failure modes (e.g., bias toward easy queries despite the rescue loop, template-enforced query phrasing reducing linguistic diversity) are not deeply analyzed.

Scope is narrower than the 'generalist' framing suggests: only tabular/sqlite data files, reasoning-oriented tasks only (no training, prediction, or visualization tasks), Qwen-family backbones up to 14B, and ~350 RL steps due to compute limits. The bold SOTA claims in the abstract/figures (Fig. 1b) are stronger than what the scoped evaluation fully supports.

Contamination analysis is coarse (table-header overlap only); semantic-level leakage between harvested Kaggle files and benchmark data is not ruled out. Also, the self-consistency filtering ablation in Fig. 4 lacks error bars/statistical significance despite 3-trial evaluation, and some conclusions (e.g., 'random-select on par with best-select') are drawn from single-seed runs.

Some claims are under-supported or stylistically overreaching (e.g., 'the greatest truths are the simplest', 'first to systematically investigate scaling of agent post-training in the data-analytic scenario' — the 'scaling' evidence rests on a 2K/4K/8K/12K ablation).

strengths: Comprehensive end-to-end pipeline covering data synthesis, trajectory curation, and multi-turn RL training for data-analytic agents, with each stage (query taxonomy, self-consistency filtering, dynamic SFT/RL weighting, memory-frugal rollout) concretely described and grounded in the ReAct setting.

Strong empirical results: the trained 7B/14B models substantially outperform both untrained open-source backbones (11.26% -> 68-71% average) and specialized baselines (TableLLM, Table-R1, OmniSQL, SQL-R1), including on these baselines' home benchmarks, with larger training corpora.

Thoughtful analysis section: the ablations on self-consistency filtering vs. trajectory selection, the dual role of SFT loss in RL training (stabilizer vs. exploration suppressor, with entropy curves), and the RL-vs-cold-start scaling experiments provide genuinely useful empirical insights.

Extra due-diligence beyond the main table: judge-model consistency check with Qwen-2.5-72B (Pearson 0.96), Rouge-L cross-check, data-contamination (header-overlap) analysis, evaluation on an additional benchmark (QRData), an additional base model family (Llama-3.1-8B), and a baseline-scaffold comparison (Data Interpreter).
Hyperparameters, prompts, and baseline reproduction protocols are documented in detail in the appendix.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the core components are largely assembled from existing work - ReAct, self-consistency filtering, DAPO, and the dynamic SFT/RL weighting is directly adopted from Zhang et al. (2025b). The paper is a well-executed application rather than a methodological advance, and the 'first to systematically investigate scaling of agent post-training' claim is overreaching.

The headline claim of 'outperforming proprietary baselines DeepSeek-V3.1 and GPT-5' is fragile. All baselines are evaluated in a uniform zero-shot ReAct scaffold at temperature 0.7 with GPT-4o-mini judging - a configuration likely unfavorable to strong reasoning models - and no effort is made to tune baseline prompting or scaffolds. Moreover the training data itself is generated and judged using the strongest baseline (DeepSeek-V3.1) plus GPT-4o-mini, so the result may largely reflect distillation plus in-domain training rather than a generalist agent exceeding frontier models.

Evaluation protocol concerns: the authors replace the original metrics of all three benchmarks with their own model-as-judge (GPT-4o-mini), which is also used as the training reward; scores are therefore not comparable to any previously reported numbers. BIRD validation set is used as testbed, TableBench is filtered, and exact-match on materialized CSVs replaces SQL execution. The judge-validation ablation is encouraging but is run on only two datasets and does not eliminate train/eval reward entanglement.

The 'scaling' framing is weakly supported: only ~12K trajectories, two Qwen backbones capped at 14B, ~350 RL steps, and one additional 8B model family. The data-volume ablation (2K-12K) shows gains but is far from demonstrating a scaling law; the limitations section concedes the scope (tabular data only, no visualization/prediction/ML tasks).

Some reported effects lack rigor: SFT-then-RL and zero-RL baselines reportedly 'collapse' and require checkpoint selection on a validation set, blurring the SFT-and-RL comparison in Table 2; the seed/variance across 3 trials is not reported; and the conclusion that self-consistency filtering beats best-trajectory selection is partly confounded by training-set size, as the authors themselves admit.

Reproducibility gaps: no public code or model links in the manuscript (footnote is empty); full dataset and models are promised only after the review period, with only a 3,843-instance subset available now. Contamination analysis is limited to table-header overlap, which is a coarse proxy.
Significance is bounded: the recipe is confined to tabular, code-based EDA tasks; whether the insights transfer to broader agentic domains is asserted rather than shown.

strengths: Comprehensive and well-motivated pipeline covering the full lifecycle of data-analytic agent construction: data file collection, query synthesis with a fine-grained 18-category taxonomy, knowledge-augmented trajectory sampling with self-consistency filtering, and a hybrid SFT+RL training objective.

Strong empirical results: DataMind-14B reportedly outperforms strong proprietary baselines (GPT-5, DeepSeek-V3.1) and all open-source competitors across three benchmarks, with substantial gains over trained baselines using far smaller training corpora (12K vs. up to 2.5M instances).

Unusually thorough analysis and validation: ablations on data volume, training strategy (SFT vs. zero-RL vs. SFT-then-RL vs. hybrid), trajectory filtering/selection, gamma scheduling with entropy dynamics, cold-start effects, an external judge-model agreement check (Pearson r=0.96), a Rouge-L cross-check, and a data contamination (header-overlap) analysis.

Good generality evidence: the pipeline transfers to Llama-3.1-8B, additional baselines (Data Interpreter) and an extra benchmark (QRData) are included in the appendix, and the analysis yields actionable insights (e.g., self-consistency filtering > best-trajectory selection; RL narrows but does not reverse base-model gaps).

Good reproducibility posture: hyperparameters, prompts, and evaluation protocols are detailed; code and a data subset are submitted, with full data/models promised post-review; feasibility demonstrated on 8x80G A100s within 2 days.
weaknesses: Limited technical novelty: the main ingredients (ReAct, self-consistency filtering, DAPO, dynamic SFT/RL weighting from Zhang et al., 2025b, entropy-collapse mitigation) are largely existing techniques recombined for a new domain; the contribution is primarily engineering and empirical rather than methodological.

Evaluation protocols deviate from original benchmark setups in ways that may favor the authors: TableBench's official Rouge-L metric is replaced by model-as-judge, BIRD's test set is substituted by its validation set, and tables are converted to .sqlite across benchmarks. The SOTA-over-GPT-5 claim therefore rests on re-scored, modified benchmarks.

The GPT-4o-mini judge is used both as the RL reward signal and as the evaluation metric, creating a potential train/test reward-hacking circularity; the external-judge (Qwen-2.5-72B) check mitigates but does not fully eliminate this concern, and judge cost/variance across three trials is not reported.

No statistical significance testing, error bars, or variance over multiple training runs are reported; some conclusions (e.g., hybrid training stability advantages, pass@1 vs. pass@3 gap narrowing) rest on single runs, and the authors admit checkpoint selection on a validation set for unstable baselines.

Backbone coverage is narrow in the main results (Qwen-2.5-Coder only, capped at 14B); the Llama-8B transfer experiment is limited to a 14K-subset setting. 'First to systematically investigate scaling of agent post-training' claims are strong given concurrent work in adjacent agentic domains.

Scope restrictions acknowledged but significant: tasks limited to reasoning-oriented tabular/textual analysis (no prediction, training, or visualization), and RL limited to ~350 steps, which weakens the generality of the 'scaling' narrative.
